full_judgment:
9. Suresh Chandra Banerjee deposed as D.W. 2. He did not contest the suit by filing written statement. He stated that he was deposing in support of the case of defendant No. 1. He gave the genealogy and that the property originally belonged to Ishan Chandra, who died leaving behind two daughters Bama Sundari and Shyama Sundari. Both the daughters were married to one Mahesh Chandra. Jnan Ranjan Banerjee was the son through Bama Sundari and Niranjan Banerjee was the son through Shyama Sundari. He is the son of Niranjan. According to him Jnan Ranjan had two sons Nayan Ranjan and Pran Ranjan. Pran Ranjan died unmarried during the lifetime of his father and Nayan Ranjan died issueless after his father. After their death the property devolved upon Niranjan entirely and he is the sole heir of Niranjan. Monoranjan according to him was not a son of Jnan Ranjan. He, however, corrected himself in cross-examination by saying that Monoranjan was the adopted son of Jnan Ranjan. Then in re-examination corrected himself again by saying that Monoranjan was not an adopted son but foster son of Jnan Ranjan. He admitted that he had no paper to show that property, at any time before, stood in the name of his father or in his name. He conceded that he had no paper to show possession of himself or of his father prior to 1950. He stated that he used to reside in the holding No. 6 with Monoranjan, Shanti and Kumud between 1920 and 1950. He admitted that he appeared for the first time in the scene in 1956 when he stated that he filed an objection to the Evacuee Property authority but he could not file any paper to show that he really filed any objection in 1956. He stated that he knew defendant No. 1 5/6 years before partition, who was an inhabitant of adjoining village. He stated that after the sale of the suit property he resided with the defendant No. 1 at Hrishikesh Das Road. His father died in 1928. He denied in cross-examination that he got his name mutated in the Municipal records in collusion with the defendant No. 1 and Settlement employees. He stated that the deed of give Ext. 8 dated 6.12.18 was created by the plaintiff. He was confronted with Ext 4 C.S. Khatian which stood in the name of Jnan Ranjan and later Monoranjan recorded his name in the Municipality Ext. 5 and obtained permission for further construction dated 4.10.29 (Ext, 10). 

 13. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed argued on the point that the plaintiff is just a tenant and she could not claim any better title nor acquire any right of occupancy in such property and the law says that "she shall not be entitled to hold over possession after expiry of the period of lease" and further sub-section (4) says: "she shall be liable to be evicted without notice from such property at the expiry of the terms of the lease." This contention is begging the particular point. The property is not an enemy properly. The restrictive provisions have no manner of application. The point now comes to focus who is the owner of the property. It is evidence that the plaintiff and her husband are in occupation since 1947 as a tenant of the sons of Monoranjan Banerjee. The title of Monoranjan Banerjee and his son apparently is so clear that even no attempt was made by the defendant to assail these documents in support of the title. As has been mentioned Ext. 4 is the C.S. Khatian which stands in the name of Jnan Ranjan. On 6.12.18 Jnan Ranjan gifted the property to his son Monoranjan with authority to make further construction (Ext. 8) Monorajan recorded his name in the Municipality (Ext. 5) and obtained sanction for further construction on 4.10.29 (Ext. 10) The evidence of Ramani Mohan Dutta (P.W. 2) shows that Monorannjan died in said premises. P.W. 3 Lakmi Kanta Pal, an Advocate stated that Monoranjan was his senior and the said holding belonged to him. On the face of the documents and oral evidence Mr. Istiaq Ahmed simply contended that Monoranjan might have been gifted a portion of the suit property but the other portion belonged to Niranjan and the share of Niranjan devolved upon his son Suresh. Here lies the crux of the problem. Suresh then must prove his title in a Civil Court. As a matter of fact Evacuee Management Committee advised him accordingly because Santi Ranjan son of Monoranjan challenged his title. Without doing so. Suresh resorted to transfer his share to Talukder. The plaintiff challenged the order of the Custodian for handing over possession to Suresh. Hence she claimed adversely against both Suresh and Talukder. It is contended that plaintiff is entitled to claim adverse possession against the defendant Suresh and his vendee Talukder and precisely that in what they contended in the trial court. The High Court Division, however, unfortunately missed the point as to the right of adverse possession. The plaintiff is not a trespasser. She and her husband were tenants of the owners since 1947 and after 1953 they paid rent to the Management Committee and thereafter to the Custodian, Enemy Property. Her possession is therefore legal possession which can be termed as juridical possession. She did not get possession either by fraud or by force. She is a tenant in possession and cannot be terminologically considered as a squatter nor a way-farer or trespasser. When the Custodian, Enemy Properly released the property on the ground that the same is not Enemy Property he could not direct the plaintiff to release the property to a particular individual whose title is denied by the owner. As has been noticed that Santi Ranjan objected to the petition of Suresh Chandra in 1961 and the Management Committee advised Suresh Chandra to establish his title in a Court of law. Instead of doing so, it seems, he waited since 1961 and started paying rent in his name from 1961 and mutated his name in the S.A. Khatian which was challenged by the plaintiff as collusive. The plaintiff is holding adversely to Suresh Chandra and his vendee Shamaul Huq Talukder who allegedly stepped into shoes of his vendor but unless Suresh has established his title Talukder is just no body. In Varada Pilliai Vs. Jeevarathaal AIR 1919 PC 44 it was held that where one of the heirs of the donor holds possession as donee under an imperfect gift and subsequently the donor dies and succession opens to the other heirs also, the character of the possession of the donee which was adverse does not cease to be so by reason of his becoming a part owner along with other heirs. In this case, the gift to Monoranjan was made in 1918 and the heirs of Monoranjan exercised their right, title and interest and the plaintiff was the tenant of the sons of Monoranjan since 1947 and the attempt of Suresh for securing 'the release of the property from Evacuee Management Committee was challenged by the sons of Monoranjan. These facts indicate that the plea of adverse possession against Suresh had been taken on formidable grounds even assuming, but not holding, that Suresh became part owner through Niranjan. The Trial Court therefore rightly decreed the suit and this point unfortunately were missed by the High Court Division.
